claim: Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC) is a devastating lysosomal storage disease characterized by abnormal cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes.
source: Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC) is a devastating lysosomal storage disease characterized by abnormal cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC disease characteristics.

claim: Currently, there is no treatment for NPC.
source: Currently, there is no treatment for NPC.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of NPC treatment options.

claim: TFEB is a member of the microphthalmia transcription factors (MiTF).
source: Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a member of the microphthalmia transcription factors (MiTF), has emerged as a master regulator of lysosomal function and promoted the clearance of substrates stored in cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TFEB classification.

claim: TFEB has emerged as a master regulator of lysosomal function and promoted the clearance of substrates stored in cells.
source: Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a member of the microphthalmia transcription factors (MiTF), has emerged as a master regulator of lysosomal function and promoted the clearance of substrates stored in cells.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific literature on TFEB function.

claim: It is not known whether TFEB plays a role in cholesterol clearance in NPC disease.
source: However, it is not known whether TFEB plays a role in cholesterol clearance in NPC disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of TFEB, but not TFE3, facilitates cholesterol clearance in various NPC1 cell models.
source: Here, we show that transgenic overexpression of TFEB, but not TFE3 (another member of MiTF family) facilitates cholesterol clearance in various NPC1 cell models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sulforaphane (SFN) is a previously identified natural small-molecule TFEB agonist.
source: Pharmacological activation of TFEB by sulforaphane (SFN), a previously identified natural small-molecule TFEB agonist by us, can dramatically ameliorate cholesterol accumulation in human and mouse NPC1 cell models.
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: SFN can dramatically ameliorate cholesterol accumulation in human and mouse NPC1 cell models.
source: Pharmacological activation of TFEB by sulforaphane (SFN), a previously identified natural small-molecule TFEB agonist by us, can dramatically ameliorate cholesterol accumulation in human and mouse NPC1 cell models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 5.

claim: In NPC1 cells, SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent but MTOR-independent pathway.
source: In NPC1 cells, SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent but MTOR-independent pathway and upregulates the expression of TFEB-downstream genes, promoting lysosomal exocytosis and biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F, G, H, I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, 4.

claim: SFN upregulates the expression of TFEB-downstream genes in NPC1 cells.
source: In NPC1 cells, SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent but MTOR-independent pathway and upregulates the expression of TFEB-downstream genes, promoting lysosomal exocytosis and biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SFN promotes lysosomal exocytosis and biogenesis in NPC1 cells.
source: In NPC1 cells, SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent but MTOR-independent pathway and upregulates the expression of TFEB-downstream genes, promoting lysosomal exocytosis and biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Genetic inhibition of TFEB abolishes the cholesterol clearance and exocytosis effect by SFN.
source: While genetic inhibition of TFEB abolishes the cholesterol clearance and exocytosis effect by SFN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the NPC1 mouse model, SFN dephosphorylates/activates TFEB in the brain.
source: In the NPC1 mouse model, SFN dephosphorylates/activates TFEB in the brain and exhibits potent efficacy of rescuing the loss of Purkinje cells and body weight.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: SFN exhibits potent efficacy of rescuing the loss of Purkinje cells in the NPC1 mouse model.
source: In the NPC1 mouse model, SFN dephosphorylates/activates TFEB in the brain and exhibits potent efficacy of rescuing the loss of Purkinje cells and body weight.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: SFN exhibits potent efficacy of rescuing body weight loss in the NPC1 mouse model.
source: In the NPC1 mouse model, SFN dephosphorylates/activates TFEB in the brain and exhibits potent efficacy of rescuing the loss of Purkinje cells and body weight.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Lysosomes are essential organelles for the degradation and recycle of damaged complex substrates and organelles.
source: Lysosomes are essential organelles for the degradation and recycle of damaged complex substrates and organelles (Xu and Ren, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu and Ren, 2015.

claim: Lysosomes have emerging roles in plasma membrane repair, external environmental sensing, autophagic cargo sensing, and proinflammatory response.
source: In recent years, lysosomes have emerging roles in plasma membrane repair, external environmental sensing, autophagic cargo sensing, and proinflammatory response, thereby regulating fundamental processes such as cellular clearance and autophagy (Tsunemi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsunemi et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding lysosomal proteins could result in more than approximately 70 different lysosomal storage disorders.
source: Mutations in genes encoding lysosomal proteins could result in more than approximately 70 different lysosomal storage disorders (Fraldi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fraldi et al., 2016.

claim: NPC is a rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutation in either NPC1 or NPC2 gene.
source: Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutation in either NPC1 or NPC2 gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC disease etiology.

claim: Deficiency in NPC1 or NPC2 protein results in late endosomal/lysosomal accumulation of unesterified cholesterol.
source: Deficiency in NPC1 or NPC2 protein results in late endosomal/lysosomal accumulation of unesterified cholesterol (Sarkar et al., 2013; Spampanato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarkar et al., 2013 and Spampanato et al., 2013.

claim: Clinical symptoms of NPC include hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurodegeneration, and central nervous system dysfunction.
source: Clinical symptoms of NPC include hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurodegeneration, and central nervous system dysfunction, that is, seizure, motor impairment, and decline of intellectual function (Carstea et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carstea et al., 1997.

claim: There is no FDA-approved specific therapy for NPC.
source: So far there is no FDA-approved specific therapy for NPC, although miglustat, approved to treat type I Gaucher disease, has been used for NPC treatment in countries, including China, Canada, and the European Union (Pineda et al., 2009; Pineda et al., 2010; Wraith et al., 2010; Chien et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pineda et al., 2009; Pineda et al., 2010; Wraith et al., 2010; Chien et al., 2013.

claim: Miglustat has been used for NPC treatment in China, Canada, and the European Union.
source: So far there is no FDA-approved specific therapy for NPC, although miglustat, approved to treat type I Gaucher disease, has been used for NPC treatment in countries, including China, Canada, and the European Union (Pineda et al., 2009; Pineda et al., 2010; Wraith et al., 2010; Chien et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pineda et al., 2009; Pineda et al., 2010; Wraith et al., 2010; Chien et al., 2013.

claim: TFEB is identified as a master regulator of lysosome and autophagy by controlling the 'coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation' (CLEAR) network.
source: Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a member of the microphthalmia/TFE transcription factor (MiTF) family, is identified as a master regulator of lysosome and autophagy by controlling the 'coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation' (CLEAR) network, covering genes associated to lysosomal exocytosis and biogenesis, and autophagy (Sardiello and Ballabio, 2009; Martini-Stoica et al., 2016; Napolitano and Ballabio, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sardiello and Ballabio, 2009; Martini-Stoica et al., 2016; Napolitano and Ballabio, 2016.

claim: In normal conditions, TFEB is phosphorylated by mTOR kinase and kept in cytosol inactively.
source: In normal conditions, TFEB is phosphorylated by mTOR kinase and kept in cytosol inactively (Martina and Puertollano, 2018, Napolitano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martina and Puertollano, 2018, Napolitano et al., 2018.

claim: Under stress conditions, TFEB is dephosphorylated and actively translocates into the nucleus, promoting the expression of genes associated with lysosome and autophagy.
source: Under stress conditions, that is, starvation or oxidative stress, TFEB is dephosphorylated and actively translocates into the nucleus, promoting the expression of genes associated with lysosome and autophagy (Medina et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Puertollano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Medina et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Puertollano et al., 2018.

claim: TFEB overexpression or activation results in increased number of lysosomes, autophagy flux, and exocytosis.
source: TFEB overexpression or activation results in increased number of lysosomes, autophagy flux, and exocytosis (Medina et al., 2011; Settembre et al., 2011; Giatromanolaki et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2020), which may trigger cellular clearance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Medina et al., 2011; Settembre et al., 2011; Giatromanolaki et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2020.

claim: TFEB overexpression promotes cellular clearance and ameliorates the phenotypes in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases.
source: In fact, it is reported that TFEB overexpression promotes cellular clearance and ameliorates the phenotypes in a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's (Sardiello et al., 2009; Tsunemi and La Spada, 2012; Decressac and Björklund, 2013; Polito et al., 2014; Ballabio, 2016; Napolitano and Ballabio, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sardiello et al., 2009; Tsunemi and La Spada, 2012; Decressac and Björklund, 2013; Polito et al., 2014; Ballabio, 2016; Napolitano and Ballabio, 2016.

claim: Upregulation of TFEB has been reported to benefit lysosomal storage diseases, such as Pompe disease.
source: Moreover, upregulation of TFEB has been reported to benefit lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs), such as Pompe disease (Argüello et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Argüello et al., 2021.

claim: In HeLa NPC1 cells overexpressing TFEB-mCherry or TFEBS211A-mCherry, the cellular cholesterol levels were significantly diminished compared to non-expressed or mCherry-only transfected NPC1 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B, in HeLa NPC1 cells overexpressing TFEB-mCherry or TFEBS211A-mCherry (S211 non-phosphorylatable mutant, a constitutively active TFEB) (Wang et al., 2015), the cellular cholesterol levels (filipin) were significantly diminished compared to non-expressed or mCherry-only transfected NPC1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B, and citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: TFE3-GFP overexpression displayed no obvious reduction of cholesterol levels in HeLa NPC1 cells.
source: In contrast, TFE3-GFP overexpression displayed no obvious reduction of cholesterol levels in HeLa NPC1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: U18666A treatment significantly increased filipin signals in bright perinuclear granules, which were well co-localized with lysosomal marker LAMP1, but not with ER marker calnexin in HeLa cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1C and D, U18666A treatment significantly increased filipin signals in bright perinuclear granules, which were well co-localized with lysosomal marker LAMP1, but not with ER marker calnexin in HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that U18666A-induced cholesterol accumulation presents in the late endosome/lysosome compartment, but not in ER.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: U18666A-induced cholesterol accumulation presents in the late endosome/lysosome compartment, but not in ER.
source: As shown in Figure 1C and D, U18666A treatment significantly increased filipin signals in bright perinuclear granules, which were well co-localized with lysosomal marker LAMP1, but not with ER marker calnexin in HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that U18666A-induced cholesterol accumulation presents in the late endosome/lysosome compartment, but not in ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data shown in Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When HeLa NPC1 cells were challenged with SFN (15 μM, 12–24 h), a dramatic reduction of cholesterol accumulation by more than 30% was observed in lysosomes.
source: Moreover, when HeLa NPC1 cells were further challenged with SFN (15 μM, 12–24 h), a dramatic reduction of cholesterol accumulation (filipin intensity) by more than 30% was observed in lysosomes (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: U18666A interferes with the egress of free cholesterol from endosomes/lysosomes.
source: These results confirmed that U18666A interferes with the egress of free cholesterol from endosomes/lysosomes as previously reported by others (Lange and Steck, 1994; Davis et al., 2021) and SFN reduces lysosomal cholesterol in NPC1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lange and Steck, 1994; Davis et al., 2021.

claim: SFN reduces lysosomal cholesterol in NPC1 cells.
source: These results confirmed that U18666A interferes with the egress of free cholesterol from endosomes/lysosomes as previously reported by others (Lange and Steck, 1994; Davis et al., 2021) and SFN reduces lysosomal cholesterol in NPC1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E.

claim: SFN activates TFEB via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-mediated but MTOR-independent mechanism.
source: In our previous study, we identified that SFN activates TFEB via a ROS-Ca2+- calcineurin-mediated but MTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase)-independent mechanism (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: In HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN (15 μM, 24 h) induced robust TFEB translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus.
source: In HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN (15 μM, 24 h) induced robust TFEB translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: SFN treatment (15 μM, 24 h) resulted in an increase in the mRNA levels of TFEB downstream genes, including ULK1, SQSTM1, ATG5, and LAMP1.
source: SFN treatment (15 μM, 24 h) also resulted in an increase in the mRNA levels of TFEB downstream genes, including genes required for autophagy (ULK1, SQSTM1, and ATG5) and lysosome biogenesis-LAMP1, using quantitative real-time PCR (Q-PCR) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: BAPTA-AM, FK506 and cyclosporin A, and N-acetylcysteine can robustly block SFN-induced TFEB nuclear translocation in HeLa NPC1 cells.
source: Consistent with previous findings, BAPTA-AM (a membrane-permeable Ca2+ chelator), FK506 and cyclosporin A (CsA) (calcineurin inhibitors), and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a ROS scavenger) can robustly block SFN-induced TFEB nuclear translocation in HeLa NPC1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that in NPC1 cells SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent mechanism
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In NPC1 cells SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent mechanism.
source: Consistent with previous findings, BAPTA-AM (a membrane-permeable Ca2+ chelator), FK506 and cyclosporin A (CsA) (calcineurin inhibitors), and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a ROS scavenger) can robustly block SFN-induced TFEB nuclear translocation in HeLa NPC1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that in NPC1 cells SFN induces TFEB nuclear translocation via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-dependent mechanism
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Following 24 h exposure to SFN, S211, and S142-TFEB phosphorylation were significantly decreased.
source: Following 24 h exposure to SFN, S211, and S142-TFEB phosphorylation were significantly decreased (Figure 1I and J), while S122 phosphorylation was not affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: S122 phosphorylation of TFEB was not affected by SFN treatment.
source: Following 24 h exposure to SFN, S211, and S142-TFEB phosphorylation were significantly decreased (Figure 1I and J), while S122 phosphorylation was not affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: TFEB is dephosphorylated at S211 and S142 residues by SFN in HeLa NPC1 model.
source: These results indicate that TFEB is dephosphorylated at S211 and S142 residues by SFN in HeLa NPC1 model.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: No significant inhibition of phosphorylated MTOR or RPS6KB1 can be observed in HeLa NPC1 cells treated with SFN (15 μM, 24 h).
source: Consistently, no significant inhibition of phosphorylated MTOR (p-MTOR) or RPS6KB1 (p-RPS6KB1) can be observed in HeLa NPC1 cells treated with SFN (15 μM, 24 h) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In HeLa NPC1 cells SFN-induced TFEB activation is unlikely to be mediated by MTOR inhibition.
source: Therefore, in HeLa NPC1 cells SFN-induced TFEB activation is unlikely to be mediated by MTOR inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment did not affect NPC1 expression in human NPC1-patient fibroblasts.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment did not affect NPC1 expression in human NPC1-patient fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: SFN (15 μM, 24 h) induced robust Nrf2 nuclear translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus in HeLa NPC1 and NPC primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6, SFN (15 μM, 24 h) induced robust Nrf2 nuclear translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus in HeLa NPC1 and NPC primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In NPC1 KD HeLa cells with more than 80% knockdown efficiency, SFN can induce TFEB nuclear translocation.
source: In NPC1 KD HeLa cells with more than 80% knockdown efficiency (Figure 2A), SFN can induce TFEB nuclear translocation (Figure 2B and C) and upregulate its downstream gene expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B, C, and D.

claim: SFN can upregulate TFEB downstream gene expression in NPC1 KD HeLa cells.
source: In NPC1 KD HeLa cells with more than 80% knockdown efficiency (Figure 2A), SFN can induce TFEB nuclear translocation (Figure 2B and C) and upregulate its downstream gene expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment significantly reduced cholesterol levels in NPC1 KD cells.
source: Notably, SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment significantly reduced cholesterol levels in NPC1 KD cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: SFN treatment robustly promoted TFEB nuclear translocation in human NPC1-patient fibroblast cells.
source: Similar results were observed in human NPC1-patient fibroblast cells. SFN treatment robustly promoted TFEB nuclear translocation (Figure 2G and H) and cholesterol clearance (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: SFN treatment robustly promoted cholesterol clearance in human NPC1-patient fibroblast cells.
source: Similar results were observed in human NPC1-patient fibroblast cells. SFN treatment robustly promoted TFEB nuclear translocation (Figure 2G and H) and cholesterol clearance (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: In the siTFEB-transfected HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN-promoted (15 μM, 24 h) cholesterol clearance was almost abolished.
source: In the siTFEB-transfected HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN-promoted (15 μM, 24 h) cholesterol clearance was almost abolished (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In scrambled siRNA-transfected NPC1 cells, the cholesterol levels were significantly reduced by more than 30% by SFN.
source: In contrast, in scrambled siRNA-transfected NPC1 cells, the cholesterol levels were significantly reduced by more than 30% by SFN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: TFEB overexpression-induced reduction of cholesterol can be further boosted about 20% by SFN treatment.
source: Notably, TFEB overexpression-induced reduction of cholesterol can be further boosted about 20% by SFN treatment (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: SFN failed to diminish cholesterol in HeLa TFEB KO cells.
source: Consistently, SFN failed to diminish cholesterol in HeLa TFEB KO cells, whereas re-expression of a recombinant TFEB restored the cholesterol clearance by SFN (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Re-expression of a recombinant TFEB restored the cholesterol clearance by SFN in HeLa TFEB KO cells.
source: Consistently, SFN failed to diminish cholesterol in HeLa TFEB KO cells, whereas re-expression of a recombinant TFEB restored the cholesterol clearance by SFN (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: TFEB is specifically required for lysosomal cholesterol reduction upon SFN treatment.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that TFEB is specifically required for lysosomal cholesterol reduction upon SFN treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: After incubation with SFN (15 μM) for 24 h, HeLa NPC1 cells exhibited a dramatic increase in the signal of LAMP1 staining in the PM compared to untreated control cells.
source: After incubation with SFN (15 μM) for 24 h, HeLa NPC1 cells exhibited a dramatic increase in the signal of LAMP1 staining in the PM (surface LAMP1 signal colocalized with DiO, a PM marker) compared to untreated control cells (Figure 4A and B), suggesting an increase of lysosomal exocytic process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: SFN treatment suggests an increase of lysosomal exocytic process in HeLa NPC1 cells.
source: After incubation with SFN (15 μM) for 24 h, HeLa NPC1 cells exhibited a dramatic increase in the signal of LAMP1 staining in the PM (surface LAMP1 signal colocalized with DiO, a PM marker) compared to untreated control cells (Figure 4A and B), suggesting an increase of lysosomal exocytic process.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: SFN promoted lysosomal exocytosis in primary macrophage cells.
source: Likewise, SFN promoted lysosomal exocytosis in primary macrophage cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase of surface LAMP1 signal by SFN was significantly reduced in TFEB KO cells.
source: In contrast, this increase of surface LAMP1 signal by SFN was significantly reduced in TFEB KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that SFN-induced lysosomal exocytosis is TFEB-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SFN-induced lysosomal exocytosis is TFEB-dependent.
source: In contrast, this increase of surface LAMP1 signal by SFN was significantly reduced in TFEB KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that SFN-induced lysosomal exocytosis is TFEB-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The levels of free cholesterol released into the medium were significantly increased with SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment compared to untreated control.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, the levels of free cholesterol released into the medium treated were significantly increased with SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment compared to untreated control, suggesting that SFN can stimulate the release of free cholesterol into the medium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SFN can stimulate the release of free cholesterol into the medium.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, the levels of free cholesterol released into the medium treated were significantly increased with SFN (15 μM, 24 h) treatment compared to untreated control, suggesting that SFN can stimulate the release of free cholesterol into the medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference of released cholesteryl ester with or without SFN treatment has not been observed.
source: Notably, the difference of released cholesteryl ester with or without SFN treatment has not been observed, and the percentage of cholesteryl ester in total cholesterol released to medium was less than 10% under all conditions tested.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The percentage of cholesteryl ester in total cholesterol released to medium was less than 10% under all conditions tested.
source: Notably, the difference of released cholesteryl ester with or without SFN treatment has not been observed, and the percentage of cholesteryl ester in total cholesterol released to medium was less than 10% under all conditions tested.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In HeLa NPC1 cells treated with SFN (15 μM, 24 h), significantly higher levels of lysosomal enzymes (NAGases and ACP) were detected in the medium compared with untreated controls, but not in TFEB KO cells.
source: In HeLa NPC1 cells treated with SFN (15 μM, 24 h), significantly higher levels of lysosomal enzymes (NAGases and ACP) were detected in the medium compared with untreated controls, but not in TFEB KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SFN induces an active movement of lysosomes toward the PM and increases lysosomal exocytosis in a TFEB-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that SFN induces an active movement of lysosomes toward the PM and increases lysosomal exocytosis in a TFEB-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: In HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN (15 μM, 12 h) treatment significantly increased the immunofluorescence intensity of LAMP1.
source: In HeLa NPC1 cells, SFN (15 μM, 12 h) treatment significantly increased the immunofluorescence intensity of LAMP1 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Significant increases of LysoTracker staining were observed in HeLa NPC1 cells following 12 h treatment with SFN (15 μM).
source: We observed significant increases of LysoTracker staining in HeLa NPC1 cells following 12 h treatment with SFN (15 μM) (Figure 4G and H) as well as in NPC1 KD cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), yet LAMP1 staining was also increased (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: SFN treatment induced significant lysosomal hyperacidity.
source: When the fluorescence ratios (pHrodo Green Dextran/CF555) were calibrated to pH values, we found that SFN treatment induced significant lysosomal hyperacidity (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: SFN promotes lysosome function and biogenesis in human NPC1 model cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that SFN promotes lysosome function and biogenesis in human NPC1 model cells, consistent with our previous report.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4E-J and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TFEB expression levels in both NPC cell models were significantly decreased compared to WT.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, TFEB expression levels in both NPC cell models were significantly decreased compared to WT, indicating that TFEB expression may be inhibited in NPC cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TFEB expression may be inhibited in NPC cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, TFEB expression levels in both NPC cell models were significantly decreased compared to WT, indicating that TFEB expression may be inhibited in NPC cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The basal levels of lysosome biogenesis in NPC cells were comparable with WT cells.
source: Interestingly, the basal levels of lysosome biogenesis in NPC cells were comparable with WT cells (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggestive of compensatory changes caused by TFEB downregulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Compensatory changes may be caused by TFEB downregulation in NPC cells.
source: Interestingly, the basal levels of lysosome biogenesis in NPC cells were comparable with WT cells (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggestive of compensatory changes caused by TFEB downregulation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 24 h dramatically increased TFEB nuclei signal in the Npc1-/- MEF cells.
source: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 24 h dramatically increased TFEB nuclei signal in the Npc1-/- MEF cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 72 h exhibited substantial cholesterol reduction in Npc1-/- MEF cells.
source: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 72 h exhibited substantial cholesterol reduction, whereas SFN treatment for 24 h showed a relatively weaker cholesterol clearance in MEF cells (Figure 5C and D) compared with human NPC1 cells (Figure 1C), suggesting that human NPC cells are more sensitive to SFN treatment compared to mouse NPC cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: SFN treatment for 24 h showed a relatively weaker cholesterol clearance in MEF cells compared with human NPC1 cells.
source: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 72 h exhibited substantial cholesterol reduction, whereas SFN treatment for 24 h showed a relatively weaker cholesterol clearance in MEF cells (Figure 5C and D) compared with human NPC1 cells (Figure 1C), suggesting that human NPC cells are more sensitive to SFN treatment compared to mouse NPC cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, D and Figure 1C.

claim: Human NPC cells are more sensitive to SFN treatment compared to mouse NPC cells.
source: SFN (15 μM) treatment for 72 h exhibited substantial cholesterol reduction, whereas SFN treatment for 24 h showed a relatively weaker cholesterol clearance in MEF cells (Figure 5C and D) compared with human NPC1 cells (Figure 1C), suggesting that human NPC cells are more sensitive to SFN treatment compared to mouse NPC cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C, D and Figure 1C.

claim: Following 24 h treatment with SFN (15 μM), a significant increase of LAMP1 staining was observed in Npc1-/- MEF cells.
source: Following 24 h treatment with SFN (15 μM), a significant increase of LAMP1 staining (Figure 5E and F) and LysoTracker intensity (Figure 5G and H) were observed in Npc1-/- MEF cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Following 24 h treatment with SFN (15 μM), a significant increase of LysoTracker intensity was observed in Npc1-/- MEF cells.
source: Following 24 h treatment with SFN (15 μM), a significant increase of LAMP1 staining (Figure 5E and F) and LysoTracker intensity (Figure 5G and H) were observed in Npc1-/- MEF cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: SFN regulates TFEB-mediated lysosomal function axis and promotes cellular cholesterol clearance in NPC MEF cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that SFN regulates TFEB-mediated lysosomal function axis and promotes cellular cholesterol clearance in NPC MEF cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SFN is reportedly BBB-permeable.
source: Considering that SFN promotes lysosomal cholesterol clearance in both human and murine NPC1 cell models (Figures 1, 2 and 5) and reportedly penetrates blood–brain barrier (BBB) (Kim et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2019; Tavakkoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2019; Tavakkoli et al., 2019.

claim: A significant decrease of pS211-TFEB protein in brain tissues was observed with SFN treatment compared to vehicle.
source: As shown in Figure 6A and B, we observed a significant decrease of pS211-TFEB protein in brain tissues with SFN treatment compared to vehicle, suggesting that TFEB in the brain was directly targeted by SFN treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: TFEB in the brain was directly targeted by SFN treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 6A and B, we observed a significant decrease of pS211-TFEB protein in brain tissues with SFN treatment compared to vehicle, suggesting that TFEB in the brain was directly targeted by SFN treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: This is the first time that SFN was shown to directly active TFEB in the brain.
source: This is the first time that SFN was shown to directly active TFEB in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Daily injection of SFN (50 mg/kg) in Npc1 mice prevented a degree of Purkinje cell loss, particularly in the lobule IV/V of cerebellum.
source: As shown in Figure 6C and D, little survival of Purkinje cells in vehicle-treated Npc1-/- cerebellum, in contrast, daily injection of SFN (50 mg/kg) in Npc1 mice prevented a degree of Purkinje cell loss, particularly in the lobule IV/V of cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Daily intraperitoneal injection of SFN (50 mg/kg) exhibited a significant improvement in weight loss of Npc1 mice.
source: Notably, we observed that daily intraperitoneal injection of SFN (50 mg/kg) exhibited a significant improvement in weight loss of Npc1 mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: SFN treatment has no effect on the liver and spleen enlargement of Npc1 mice.
source: However, SFN treatment has no effect on the liver and spleen enlargement of Npc1 mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated but data is not shown.

claim: Pharmacological activation of TFEB by small-molecule agonist can mitigate NPC neuropathological symptoms in vivo.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrated that pharmacological activation of TFEB by small-molecule agonist can mitigate NPC neuropathological symptoms in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Purkinje cells located in the cerebellum are the most susceptible to NPC1 loss and exhibit a significant selective loss in the anterior part of the cerebellum.
source: Purkinje cells located in the cerebellum are the most susceptible to NPC1 loss and exhibit a significant selective loss in the anterior part of the cerebellum (Sarna et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sarna et al., 2003.

claim: Typically, Npc1 mice weight plateaus at 6–7 weeks of age, and then progressively declines.
source: Typically, Npc1 mice weight plateaus at 6–7 weeks of age, and then progressively declines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Npc1 mice phenotype.

claim: Overexpression of TFEB, but not TFE3, alleviated lysosomal cholesterol accumulation in NPC cells.
source: Surprisingly, in this study we found that overexpression of TFEB, but not TFE3, alleviated lysosomal cholesterol accumulation in NPC cells (Figure 1A and B Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only TFEB overexpression, but not other MiT members, upregulates lysosomal gene expression.
source: Moreover, studies reported that only TFEB overexpression, but not other MiT members, upregulates lysosomal gene expression (Sardiello et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sardiello et al., 2009.

claim: The functions exerted by TFEB and TFE3 in NPC may appear to be specialized.
source: Thus, these results suggest that the functions exerted by TFEB and TFE3 in NPC may appear to be specialized.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: The concentration of SFN used in this study has no cytotoxicity toward the cell lines used.
source: The concentration of SFN used in this study has no cytotoxicity toward the cell lines we used (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: SFN is an electrophilic compound enriched in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli.
source: SFN, an electrophilic compound enriched in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, is a known potent inducer of NFE2L2/NRF2 in various cell types including NPC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), a transcriptional factor that controls the expression of multiple detoxifying enzymes through antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Yamamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SFN.

claim: SFN is a known potent inducer of NFE2L2/NRF2 in various cell types including NPC cells.
source: SFN, an electrophilic compound enriched in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, is a known potent inducer of NFE2L2/NRF2 in various cell types including NPC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), a transcriptional factor that controls the expression of multiple detoxifying enzymes through antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Yamamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and citation to Yamamoto et al., 2018.

claim: The promoter region of the Nfe2l2 gene harbors a CLEAR site, and TFEB activation can upregulate the expression of Nfe2l2.
source: Notably, the promoter region of the Nfe2l2 gene harbors a CLEAR site, and TFEB activation can upregulate the expression of Nfe2l2 (Mansueto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mansueto et al., 2017.

claim: TFEB, together with NFE2L2, functions as a key regulator of cellular redox.
source: Hence, TFEB, together with NFE2L2, functions as a key regulator of cellular redox.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and experimental data.

claim: Oxidative stress is a major feature of NPC and has been attributed to neuronal damage, leading to the pathogenesis and progression of NPC.
source: Oxidative stress is a major feature of NPC and has been attributed to neuronal damage, leading to the pathogenesis and progression of NPC (Vázquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vázquez et al., 2012.

claim: Elevated oxidative stress has been observed in the brain of NPC patient and mice.
source: Elevated oxidative stress has been observed in the brain of NPC patient and mice (Smith et al., 2009; Zampieri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2009; Zampieri et al., 2009.

claim: NPC patients show decreased antioxidant capacity and diminished activity of different antioxidant enzymes.
source: NPC patients also show decreased antioxidant capacity (expressed as Trolox equivalents) and diminished activity of different antioxidant enzymes, which indicates a decrease in antioxidant defenses (Fu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2010.

claim: The protective effect of SFN against NPC could be attributed to a combination with antioxidant activity and cholesterol clearance via the lysosome-dependent, TFEB-mediated regulation.
source: Hence, the protective effect of SFN against NPC could be attributed to a combination with antioxidant activity and cholesterol clearance via the lysosome-dependent, TFEB-mediated regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Pharmacological activation of TFEB may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy for NPC.
source: Therefore, pharmacological activation of TFEB may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy for NPC.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and discussion.

claim: U18666A is an inhibitor of the endosomal/lysosomal cholesterol transporter NPC1.
source: HeLa cells were treated with U18666A (2.5 μM, an inhibitor of the endosomal/lysosomal cholesterol transporter NPC1), a drug that has been widely used to induce NPC phenotype in cell models (Poh et al., 2012) (thereafter HeLa NPC1 cells represent U18666A-treated HeLa cells).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poh et al., 2012.

claim: U18666A has been widely used to induce NPC phenotype in cell models.
source: HeLa cells were treated with U18666A (2.5 μM, an inhibitor of the endosomal/lysosomal cholesterol transporter NPC1), a drug that has been widely used to induce NPC phenotype in cell models (Poh et al., 2012) (thereafter HeLa NPC1 cells represent U18666A-treated HeLa cells).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poh et al., 2012.

claim: Filipin is a well-known cholesterol-marker.
source: Cellular cholesterol levels were measured by the well-known cholesterol-marker filipin (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015.

claim: TFEBS211A is a constitutively active TFEB.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B, in HeLa NPC1 cells overexpressing TFEB-mCherry or TFEBS211A-mCherry (S211 non-phosphorylatable mutant, a constitutively active TFEB) (Wang et al., 2015), the cellular cholesterol levels (filipin) were significantly diminished compared to non-expressed or mCherry-only transfected NPC1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: SFN (10–15 μM, 3–24 h) potently activates TFEB in various cell lines, promoting lysosomal function.
source: Based on our previous data that SFN (10–15 μM, 3–24 h) potently activates TFEB in various cell lines, promoting lysosomal function (Li et al., 2021), thus, in this study, we set SFN treatment dose to 15 μM and treatment time to 4–24 h according to individual experiment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: SFN can mitigate oxidative stress via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-TFEB-mediated lysosomal function and autophagy flux.
source: Previously we have shown that SFN can mitigate oxidative stress via a ROS-Ca2+-calcineurin-TFEB-mediated lysosomal function and autophagy flux (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: When lysosomal exocytosis processes, luminal lysosomal membrane proteins can be detected on the extracellular side of the plasma membrane by measuring surface expression of LAMP1.
source: When lysosomal exocytosis processes, luminal lysosomal membrane proteins can be detected on the extracellular side of the plasma membrane (PM) by measuring surface expression of LAMP1 (lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1), a resident marker protein of late endosomes and lysosomes (referred to as 'lysosomes' for simplicity hereafter) with a monoclonal antibody against a luminal epitope of LAMP1 (Reddy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reddy et al., 2001.

claim: A direct consequence of lysosomal exocytosis is the release of lysosomal contents into the cell culture medium.
source: A direct consequence of lysosomal exocytosis is the release of lysosomal contents into the cell culture medium (Rodríguez et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodríguez et al., 1997.

claim: The MiT/TFE family contains four factors: MITF, TFEB, TFE3, and TFEC.
source: The MiT/TFE family contains four factors: MITF, TFEB, TFE3, and TFEC, which share an identical basic region for DNA binding, and highly similar HLH and Zip regions for dimerization (Haq and Fisher, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haq and Fisher, 2011.

claim: MiT/TFE family members share an identical basic region for DNA binding, and highly similar HLH and Zip regions for dimerization.
source: The MiT/TFE family contains four factors: MITF, TFEB, TFE3, and TFEC, which share an identical basic region for DNA binding, and highly similar HLH and Zip regions for dimerization (Haq and Fisher, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haq and Fisher, 2011.
